canberra.title: Alleged attack on schoolboy outside Lake Tuggeranong College caught on film
canberra.snippet: The ACT Magistrates Court has seen footage – apparently shared online – that shows several people fighting in a carpark outsi...
canberra.content:
13 November 2026

Ibrahim Dweiher, 18, was released on bail by the ACT Magistrates Court on Friday. Photo: Albert McKnight.

The ACT Magistrates Court has seen footage – apparently shared online – that shows several people fighting in a carpark outside a southern Canberra school in a shocking incident that included a young boy being stabbed twice.

Region has previously reported on how 18-year-old Ibrahim Dweiher and 19-year-old Soufiane Arjeuan allegedly went to Lake Tuggeranong College on the afternoon of 2 November 2026 before they approached a 16-year-old boy in the carpark.

It is alleged a verbal exchange escalated into a fight, in which Mr Arjeuan punched the boy before Mr Dweiher slashed him twice with a flick knife.

Court documents allege the boy caused Mr Dweiher to lose control of the knife, resulting in the latter receiving a deep cut to the inside of his wrist.

The brief video, which Mr Dweiher’s lawyers said hadn’t come from police but from “another source”, shows a scuffle between at least four males next to a red car in a carpark.

It appears to show Mr Dweiher being grabbed before he broke free and walked away, while the 16-year-old boy was grabbed around the head. Mr Dweiher then walked to the passenger’s side of the red car, before someone swiped at his arm.

The video was played to the Magistrates Court when Mr Dweiher applied for bail on Friday (13 November).

His barrister said when viewing the video, nothing suggested that he had been holding a weapon. In fact, another person appeared “to be waving something in his direction” when he got into the car.

The barrister argued there was a real question whether the allegations written by police were “accurate and reliable”.

Prosecutor James Melloy, who opposed bail, said the video showed the end of the incident. He said the 16-year-old boy and two witnesses claimed Mr Dweiher had a knife.

He said the boy had given the knife to a teacher after the incident. The boy had been left with a cut to his hand and a 15 cm cut to his forearm.

Mr Melloy also noted people had allegedly gone to hospital to find the 16-year-old boy after the alleged incident.

In addition, the prosecutor said police had recently told him about their concerns regarding “ongoing retributive actions” against the boy.

He said police claimed people had gone to the boy’s workplace on the weekend, while some people had also attempted to contact the boy on the phone.

“It is premeditated and deliberate offending, offending that is very violent and includes the use of a flick knife,” he alleged.

Magistrate Alexandra Burt said that, due to Mr Dweiher’s young age, lack of prior criminal history, family support and the time needed to resolve the matter, she would grant bail on numerous strict conditions that essentially amounted to house arrest.

However, he will be allowed to continue attending the Canberra Institute of Technology to continue his studies.

Mr Dweiher was charged with affray, joint commission intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm and committing an act endangering life. His matter returns to court on 24 November.

Mr Arjeuan remains in custody and has entered pleas of not guilty to affray, joint commission intentionally inflicting actual bodily harm and joint commission intentionally inflicting grievous bodily harm. He returns to court on 15 December.

canberra.title: Gun allegedly fired at car containing children in ‘horrendous’ road rage incident
canberra.snippet: Three underage teenagers were in their car when they were allegedly chased through Canberra, repeatedly rammed and even had a gun fired a...
canberra.content:
Ahmad Alrajab, 20, has been charged over an alleged road rage incident on 25 May. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Three underage teenagers were in their car when they were allegedly chased through Canberra, repeatedly rammed and even had a gun fired at them, a court has heard.

Ahmad Alrajab, a 20-year-old from Spence, and an underage co-defendant were arrested over their alleged roles earlier this year before more details about the case were revealed in the ACT Magistrates Court.

It is alleged Mr Alrajab was driving the pair in a Ford Focus on the night of 25 May 2026 when they began interacting with the three occupants, all aged under 18, of a Holden Cruze.

Mr Alrajab allegedly pulled up next to the Holden, then pursued the teens when they drove off and began ramming their car with his own.

The court heard he then allegedly drove up alongside the Holden, “lining up the shot”, before his underage co-defendant fired a gun at the car.

Mr Alrajab allegedly continued to ram the boys’ vehicle. Afterwards, it is alleged the firearm was taken back to his home.

ACT Policing has previously said the three teens were not injured during the incident.

Mr Alrajab was charged with discharging a firearm and furious driving. He has remained in custody since he was arrested later that same month, then applied for bail on Friday (13 November).

“It is horrendous behaviour,” prosecutor Taden Kelliher said when opposing bail.

“[It allegedly involves] young children, subjected to such significant violence.”

Mr Kelliher alleged the teens had identified Mr Alrajab as the driver of the Ford during a Triple Zero call made during the incident.

He claimed the defendant’s driving had been “ridiculous” and “beggars belief”.

A police officer told the court two of the three teens reported they would be extremely afraid if Mr Alrajab were granted bail.

“We’ve been unable to locate the firearm,” the officer also said.

The court was shown videos taken from the underage co-defendant’s mobile phone, which depicted someone inspecting what appeared to be a firearm.

Barrister Amarande Chauvet, appearing for Mr Alrajab, said the person holding the firearms in the videos had not been identified. She also said there was no indication whether these firearms were gel blasters or functioning guns.

Ms Chauvet said there was a question whether, on the allegations, her client was aware that there was a firearm in the car at the time of the incident.

She also said there was a real question about whether the prosecution could prove a firearm had been fired at all during the incident.

“There are uncertainties, I accept that,” Magistrate Alexandra Burt said.

But the magistrate also said the firearm from the alleged incident was still missing and Mr Alrajab was alleged to possibly have access to it, which was a significant issue for her.

Due to unrelated charges, Mr Alrajab had to demonstrate special or exceptional circumstances existed for him to apply for bail.

Magistrate Burt ultimately said he had not established that such circumstances existed and refused bail, adjourning the matter to 25 November.

The underage co-defendant is in custody and has already been committed to the Supreme Court for a trial on his charges.

canberra.title: Backflip over backpacker visas back on the agenda
canberra.snippet: Labor appears prepared to back down on its new backpacker visa policy after heavy criticism from the business sector and a ‘please explai...
canberra.content:
The hospitality industry has not been happy about Labor’s planned changes to working holiday visas and have let the government know it. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

Labor appears prepared to back down on its new backpacker visa policy after heavy criticism from the business sector and a ‘please explain’ from the United Kingdom.

The plan is set to be reviewed after the hospitality and tourism sectors, as well as agriculture, rural and small business groups, have complained they will face staff shortages if working holiday visa numbers are reduced.

Under the current free trade agreement with the UK, British backpackers can stay in Australia for up to three years without specific work having to be undertaken here.

Working Holiday Maker visas for other nationals require them to spend time working in regional areas if they want to extend their visas.

Australia was looking to extend that requirement to all backpackers, with Immigration Minister Tony Burke including the proposal in a tranche of announcements he made during his National Press Club appearance in September.

The Federal Government plans to reduce net migration to 225,000 people by 2028, bringing it down from 300,000.

In part, that would be achieved through a new ballot system for working holiday makers, with caps also being imposed on second-year visa places at 45,000 – down from 57,000 this year.

A cap would also have been placed on third-year visas at 5000, down from 31,000 this year.

On Friday (13 November), however, the minister said the government was now prepared to reconsider the backpacker policy.

“The parameters were clear – the total numbers, which I had announced in the Press Club speech, were something that I could not compromise on,” Mr Burke said.

“But if we could find a better way of getting a similar immigration outcome with a better outcome for industry, then I wanted us to work to that.

“Those conversations are continuing.”

It follows not only pressure from the hospitality and agriculture sectors, which rely heavily on itinerant workers, but also representations from Western Australian Premier Roger Cook, who wants regional work obligations reinstated for British backpackers.

Meanwhile, Anthony Albanese has met for the second time with his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, over the matter.

The two prime ministers met on the sidelines of last month’s CHOGM meeting in the Caribbean and agreed to further “discuss options”.

They have again met in Türkiye on the sidelines of the COP31 climate change summit, agreeing to negotiate any changes to the status quo.

The Greens have described Mr Burke’s latest remarks on the issue as a clear backflip.

Greens leader Senator David Shoebridge said it has exposed that Labor’s policy was based on “chasing One Nation to the right” on immigration.

“This backflip on backpackers shows that this approach to immigration policy from One Nation and Labor, of just picking a number out of the sky, doesn’t work,” Senator Shoebridge said.

“Labor, One Nation and the Coalition have all tried this, picking an arbitrary number and then watching it get picked apart by reality.

“This is why immigration policy needs to be set by core principles, not by media sound grabs.

“All across the country, communities, businesses and lives are improved by the many contributions of migrants, and this is why these anti-immigration policies simply don’t stand up to scrutiny.

“Even with this backflip, Labor still intends to block families from reuniting with loved ones, build new immigration detention centres and send hundreds of uniformed Border Force officers into communities.”

Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Andrew McKellar has welcomed the development, and confirmed that some ACCI members had been involved in “extensive discussions” the government has been holding with the most directly affected groups.

“What those groups have been trying to highlight is the potentially unintended impacts of the measures that were announced a couple of months ago by Mr Burke at the National Press Club,” he said.

“What impact they can have for those businesses, particularly in rural and regional areas where there’s a requirement at the moment that in the first year, if you come in as a backpacker, you have to work a minimum of 88 days in a regional area if you want to get a second-year visa. So I think that’s an important qualification.

“The proposals, as they were outlined, ran the risk of really creating a disincentive for people to undertake that work. And those regional areas really need those people to be coming out there and to be undertaking that work, supporting work in those areas.

“We’re just encouraging the government to make a decision here, listen to what those businesses have been telling them, and the ball is in their court; the clock is ticking; they need to act; they need to act now.”

canberra.title: Students slam ACT library cuts, but minister says fewer hours are bringing in more visitors
canberra.snippet: Canberra students are putting pressure on the ACT Government to reverse its decision to reduce the opening hours of its public libraries....
canberra.content:
An open letter with over 500 signatures, led by the lobby group Students for ACT Libraries, is putting pressure on the ACT Government to revisit its decision to reduce opening hours for its 9 public libraries. Photo: Libraries ACT.

Canberra students are putting pressure on the ACT Government to reverse its decision to reduce the opening hours of its public libraries.

In late August, the ACT Government announced it would cut late-night and Sunday opening hours across all libraries, while scrapping weekend hours entirely at Civic, Erindale and Kippax.

The decision to reduce operating hours has been widely slammed, with petitions and outcry calling on the government to reverse it; the most recent call came from the student-led group Students for ACT Libraries.

In an open letter with 500 signatures, penned for ACT Minister for City Services Tara Cheyne, Students for Libraries described ACT Libraries as important locations where visitors study, learn and connect.

“Since the changes took effect on the 27th of August 2026, there has been a significant impact on our and other Canberrans’ day-to-day lives. Libraries are valued as spaces that facilitate social cohesion, digital literacy and equitable access to information and community resources,” the letter said.

“We implore the government to: Reverse the weekend closures within ACT Libraries, expanding accessibility to our libraries; Reinstate the Giggle & Wiggle program at Kippax Library, given the resources and support it provided to the youngest members of our community; and release thorough library usage figures detailing visitation data to ensure transparency regarding future changes.

“Libraries are well-beloved community services that we feel are essential, and their removal has left a hole in our community’s ability to access the services it needs and come together.”

Ms Cheyne acknowledged the correspondence and has expressed interest in working with the group.

“I have received correspondence, including the open letter from Students for ACT Libraries,” Ms Cheyne said.

“They are right that libraries are where people study, connect and learn, and I welcome their engagement and advocacy. I look forward to meeting with the group in the coming weeks.”

Ms Cheyne said the decision to reduce opening hours and services was not made overnight.

“I understand the concern about the opening hours changes. For years, Libraries ACT’s opening hours were stretched across a patchwork of individual staffing arrangements which made it difficult to reliably staff our branches across the days they were advertised as being open,” she said.

“Branches with late nights and Sundays on paper and unplanned closures in practice were becoming commonplace.

“It is not something that I could let continue. The government decided the hours, which allowed for the roster to be redesigned with staff.

“Since 27 August, every branch opens the same core hours every weekday and Belconnen, Civic, Dickson, Gungahlin, Tuggeranong, Woden and Kingston open for full-day Saturdays.

“For the first time in years, there will be no cutback summer hours: branches will run their normal hours until 5 pm on 23 December and reopen on 4 January. Civic Library reopens in December after roof repairs.”

While the cutbacks are still a sore point for many users, Ms Cheyne said the research behind the reduced hours is public, with data suggesting more visitors since the reduction.

“The hourly door-count data was released under FOI earlier this year, and I have asked Libraries ACT to publish visitation by branch and day on an ongoing basis,” she said.

“Early figures since the change show more people coming through the doors, not fewer.

“Kippax and Erindale are the first in line for expanded access into the weekend, which we will implement from July 2027. The exact form of that model is being actively worked through.

“The Saturday Giggle and Wiggle session at Kippax has moved to Belconnen, and early figures show the attendance there is consistent with the attendance numbers at Kippax.

“Overall, Giggle and Wiggle sessions have grown, not shrunk: there are now 17 sessions a week across the network.

“However, I recognise a gain for the network overall doesn’t discount the loss for families in West Belconnen, and this is something we will look at closely as part of the evaluation.”

canberra.title: Federal Court keeps restrictions on Young electrician jailed for helping Islamic State
canberra.snippet: A Young electrician who served nine years for helping Islamic State will remain under a federal control order until March after a judge w...
canberra.content:
The Federal Court confirmed a control order restricting Young electrician Haisem Zahab’s travel, internet use and contacts until 22 March 2027. Photo: LinkedIn.

A Young electrician who served nine years for helping Islamic State will remain under a federal control order until March after a judge warned he could return to the online activity that led to his offending.

Federal Court Justice Robert Bromwich confirmed the order on 30 October after lifting an ankle monitor requirement on 9 July, finding the device could make it harder for Haisem Zahab to find work while doing little to reduce the risk he would re-engage with extremism online.

The court published its reasons on 11 November.

The order continues to restrict where he can travel, how he can use the internet and who he can contact until 22 March 2027.

Counter-terrorism police arrested the electrician, then 42, while searching his home in Young on 28 February 2017.

Andrew Colvin, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) commissioner at the time, said the arrest followed an 18-month investigation.

Working largely from his home in Young, Zahab researched rocket guidance and developed a device to warn of incoming laser-guided weapons.

He pleaded guilty to intentionally providing support or resources to Islamic State and failing to comply with an order to help police access encrypted data.

At his sentencing in 2019, NSW Supreme Court Justice Geoffrey Bellew found the research involved extensive planning and was intended to help Islamic State in armed conflicts overseas.

The judge found Zahab had gone to considerable lengths to keep the work secret and had delayed the investigation by withholding passwords he knew.

Justice Bellew imposed a nine-year prison sentence for the terrorism offence, with a non-parole period of six years and nine months.

According to the Federal Court’s reasons, he was released from Wellington Correctional Centre on 27 March 2026 after serving his full sentence without parole.

Federal police fitted the ankle monitor that day under an interim order made four days earlier.

In a 2 June affidavit, AFP Detective Superintendent Jeremy Staunton said officers had identified no breaches of the interim order and that Zahab had once volunteered to show them his online search history.

The affidavit described strong family ties, work on the farm and attendance at the local mosque, with little contact with the wider community.

Det Supt Staunton said it was too early to tell whether the risk had subsided and pointed to some of the pressures Zahab had faced before his offending, including social isolation, unemployment and financial stress.

Defence lawyers argued the risk was remote, pointing to prison records in which their client repeatedly renounced Islamic State, his participation in programs aimed at disengaging from violent extremism and his family’s support.

In a 16 June report, clinical and forensic psychologist Dr Katie Seidler found little evidence of a current risk of violent extremism requiring outside monitoring.

Justice Bromwich gave the report limited weight because it relied heavily on Zahab’s account – not tested in cross-examination because he did not give evidence at the July hearing – and did little to address the risk of future offending.

He said the evidence supported Zahab’s claim to have turned away from extremist ideology, but he could not be satisfied the change would last.

The judge accepted that a recent autism diagnosis had given Zahab a better understanding of his behaviour, although there was limited evidence about how well his strategies would work if he began to withdraw again.

Justice Bromwich found a “real and unacceptable level of risk” that he could fall back into the habits that led to his radicalisation and offend again.

Living in a rural area could add to his isolation, he said, making it important that the order give him room to work and build ties in the community.

Zahab’s lawyers said he had taken steps to renew his electrical licence and planned to train in solar panel and battery installation.

His wife said in an affidavit that the ankle monitor could discourage him from looking for work.

Justice Bromwich accepted it could be a barrier to employment and said there was no evidence of a flight risk.

The order limits his travel to NSW and the ACT and requires him to live at an approved address, with stays of up to 72 hours at a listed family address or another address approved by police permitted on at least two business days’ written notice.

Justice Bromwich said that would allow Zahab to take weekend trips with family and strengthen those relationships.

Police can monitor his online activity and require access to his devices and accounts.

He must also consider counselling or psychological treatment, which the AFP will pay for during the order if he takes it up.

Original Article published by Edwina Mason on About Regional.

australia.title: Microsoft scrambles to fix global outage affecting Teams and Outlook
australia.snippet: Tech firm says it is making progress in attempts to restore services and there is no indication problem was caused by cyber-attack Micros...
australia.content:
Microsoft is scrambling to fix an outage of some of its systems that has caused huge disruption to users, organisations and businesses across the globe.

In its latest update, the tech company said it was making progress in its attempts to restore services after a global outage affected millions of users from Thursday evening and into Friday.

The issue appears patchy, with some but not all users reporting problems with services including Microsoft Teams and Outlook email.

In an update shortly after midday GMT, Microsoft said: “We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress in Europe, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure.

“Japan remains comparatively more stable, while North America is also improving; however, some users may still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue.”

After 2pm, it added: “We’re continuing to see improvements in service availability, with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.”

More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, and more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot, Microsoft’s AI chatbot, according to the company.

Microsoft said there were no indications that the outage had been caused by a cyber-attack.

Earlier, the company said it was seeing only “marginal success” from its efforts to bring its systems fully back online. It had said that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load” – which was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors”.

The company determined a number of servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” because of a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.

The outage website Down Detector showed an increase in Microsoft 365 problems at about 6pm GMT on Thursday, with nearly 130,000 reports of problems in 74 countries affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. Copilot was also affected.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.

Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

The Microsoft outage also hit connectors used by ⁠OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI ⁠services.

OpenAI said it was investigating a problem with Microsoft connectors in which new connections may be broken and tools were not working as ⁠expected. Anthropic said it had identified an issue with an upstream provider ​affecting its Microsoft 365 ​connector.

The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.

In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several UK police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

Some schools in the UK notified parents that reporting attendance or absence issues had to be done via phone. National Rail, which provides information across the UK network, warned that people may not be able to access tickets that have been emailed to them.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffer on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

Multiple cities, including the City of Tampa, posted notices on their municipal websites to say that they are affected by the outage.

Law enforcement offices across the US have also been affected, with one sheriff’s county in Colorado saying that it is unable to process bond payments because Outlook email is down and requesting that anyone who needs to post bond do so in person.

When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.

The Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air said their email support services were affected, and Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted.

In financial markets some portfolio managers have been unable to check emails, making it hard to access on some trading platforms.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.

Microsoft last month reported an ​outage of its Azure cloud platform that affected a ​suite of productivity software ‌and a range ​of industries worldwide.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University in Melbourne, said the outage appeared to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue that brought down Optus’s network in 2023.

He said that when some of the servers had configuration issues, it meant customers were forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.

“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down. And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem, in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”

Gregory said businesses reliant on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options.

Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report

australia.title: What sinking Labor can learn from the soaring Democrats – podcast
australia.snippet: Barrie Cassidy is back from his break and keen to dive into the lessons for Australia from one of the biggest US midterm shifts in histor...
australia.content:
Barrie Cassidy is back from his break and keen to dive into the lessons for Australia from one of the biggest US midterm shifts in history. What can Labor learn from the Democrats about how to select winning – and inspiring – candidates?

Tony Barry gives his take on why the Republicans lost Texas despite being bankrolled by the richest man in the world – and why George W Bush was so pivotal to the bad result for the right wing party.

The Barries also discuss the prime minister’s trip to Turkey to attend the Cop climate conference, the newly commenced Big Build royal commission and the Victorian Liberals’ decision to preference One Nation in the upcoming state election

australia.title: Jess Wilson and the Blazing Stump: country pub voters give would-be premier a reality check (and a daiquiri)
australia.snippet: Instead of participating in a leaders debate, the Liberal took the ‘Jess Express’ to a key seat where the contest is wide open Get our br...
australia.content:
Jess Wilson has arrived at a country pub in Wodonga, on the Victorian-New South Wales border, hoping to win over voters. Her first encounter demonstrates the difficulty of this task.

Ross Reynolds tells the Victorian opposition leader that while he’s going to place the Liberal party second on his ballot paper, the first spot will go to One Nation.

He tells Wilson he desperately wants change. She counters: “The only way to change the government is to vote Liberal or Nationals.” Reynolds politely nods along but makes clear to reporters afterwards he’s not changing his vote.

“I’ve worked hard; I’m going alright, but I need to look after my grandkids,” he says, from the sports bar of the Blazing Stump Hotel.

Wilson was initially due to take part in a debate on Channel Nine on Thursday. But after neither she nor the Labor premier, Ben Carroll, could agree to the terms, and as Nine’s viewers tuned into a repeat of RBT (Random Breath Testing), the Liberal party opted to send its campaign bus, dubbed the “Jess Express”, north to sandbag a key seat.

Journalists are handed merch – on Thursday eye masks reading Wake up Ben, on Friday pen holders in the shape of Labor’s panned machete disposal bins.

Benambra has been held continuously by conservative parties since 1877 but is now sitting on a knife-edge. The retirement of the Liberal MP Bill Tilley and the decision of the independent Jacqui Hawkins not to run, after two elections spent steadily eroding a once safe margin to just 0.9%, has left the contest wide open.

The community independent movement has selected Dr Lachie McKeeman to replace Hawkins. The local Wodonga GP and volunteer firefighter says he has seen an increase in support following the alleged attack on Helen Haines, the MP for the overlapping seat of Indi.

But pollsters remain uncertain about how support will divide between McKeeman, One Nation and the Liberals. Just 10km away in New South Wales, the once safe Liberal seat turned orange at the Farrer byelection.

The Liberal party candidate, Steve Martin, a local engineer and self-proclaimed “roads nerd”, tells reporters he’s not taking anything for granted.

“There is a lot of frustration out there, and people have looked at what they’ve been delivered here in the regions, and they feel like they have been left behind. But raising the problems is a lot different to having the solution,” Martin says.

“In Jess Wilson and the leadership team, which have visited here many times, it’s not just about identifying the problems. They’ve got a plan for Victoria.”

About half of the opposition’s election pledges have been in regional Victoria, including more than $400m in the typically safe Nationals seats of Gippsland East, Lowan, Murray Plains and Ovens Valley. They have also announced more than $175m worth of election commitments for Benambra, including $50.1m to duplicate 1.7km Beechworth Road between Baranduda Boulevard and Yarralumla Drive in Leneva on Friday.

Wilson denies she is trying to buy votes.

“It’s a reflection of the fact that this Labor government has not invested in this community. Labor has been in power in this state for 21 of the past 25 years, and it has absolutely forgotten about regional Victoria,” she says.

As Wilson and Martin make the commitment, a car carrying a trailer with McKeenan’s sign drives past, and a driver screams out, “Fix the road”, and another, “Vote One Nation.”

McKeeman says he won’t presume how people plan to vote, but he has a good relationship with the One Nation candidate, Kellie Sheppard.

“We share a frustration that Benambra hasn’t been getting the representation and results it deserves. We both want to see change,” he says.

McKeeman says he hopes people considering One Nation will also look at what an independent could achieve for Benambra, pointing to people like Haines, Bob Katter and the former Shepparton MP Suzanna Sheed who “put their communities first, answer to the people who elect them and are prepared to work with anyone to deliver results”.

He describes Haines as a friend and mentor.

“Since the incident, people have really come together. I think it has reminded people of the kind of politics they want to see, with more respectful, community-minded representation focused on getting things done,” McKeeman says.

Back at the pub, Reynolds, who is in his 70s, tells reporters when he was younger, he worked in the meat industry and was a rusted-on Labor voter. But after opening his own shop, he was forced to “change his ways”, believing Labor did not support small business.

Now, he complains that Labor is “spending, spending, spending” and says there needs to be a pathway out of debt. Despite Wilson campaigning on the issue, he’s unconvinced the Liberal party will deliver on that either.

Then there are Matt and Baylin, who are based in Geelong but have spent the past three weeks on the road working in the auctioneering business, selling machinery and transport equipment.

Baylin is tight-lipped about his voting intentions. He says it is good to see Wilson “out and about among the people”, but he has yet to make up his mind and probably won’t until election day.

Matt, meanwhile, has voted Labor in the past and is still “definitely considering” voting for the party again. But the condition of regional roads has him thinking about jumping ship.

“Dodging the potholes and watching people dodging the potholes – it’s totally changed the way you drive down country roads,” he says.

He also understands why some voters are being drawn towards One Nation, as an anti-establishment vote promising “major change”.

“They’re going to really put a cat among pigeons in this election – it’s going to be like America in some respects, the Trump effect, where people might [think] … damn the main parties, we’ll go something different,” Matt says. “That will be a big factor.”

Mark Palmer and his colleagues from a modular building company based in Kilsyth are in town to add office space to Albury Wodonga Health. They are excited to see Wilson at the pub and pose for photos with her, even shouting her a strawberry daiquiri.

For Palmer, crime is the defining issue of the election.

“I’ve got two teenage daughters, and I am genuinely worried about them going out into town at night,” he says, citing the alleged murder of Feng Jianming, a food delivery driver in Melbourne’s CBD last week.

Palmer is also concerned about immigration. He says he respects migrants who have come to Australia and worked incredibly hard, but he believes immigration needs to slow down due to the strain on housing and infrastructure.

He has been considering voting for One Nation. After meeting Wilson, however, he says that may have changed.

“Her being here has probably changed my mind.”

australia.title: Vanessa delivers pizza after work to pay rent. Many Australians are ‘scrambling’ as cracks appear in the economy
australia.snippet: Australians are more worried about the economy than they have been since 2022 as interest rate hikes, price rises and job cuts fuel finan...
australia.content:
Vanessa Freitas is not feeling optimistic about her one-year-old daughter’s future in Australia.

Now an Australian citizen with a white-collar job in Sydney’s CBD, the 37-year-old worked as a nanny and house cleaner after moving from Brazil 13 years ago.

Freitas has moved at least 14 times since arriving in Australia and still can’t afford to buy a home, even though she and her partner are both professionals. They’re at their absolute limit for what they can afford to pay in rent.

“We are both on wages that should be enough, right?” she says. “But what we’re making now is barely covering the bills … I’ve started delivering pizza at night, because we are scrambling.”

She says migrants are being unfairly blamed for the housing crisis when they “contribute to this country [and] pay taxes like everyone else”.

“In terms of stability and financial stability and just having a future, I think the Australian dream is dead, especially when it comes to housing.”

Australians are more worried about the economy than they have been since 2022 and businesses reported the worst conditions since 2020, new data this week showed.

Steady price rises, interest rate hikes and recent job cuts have fuelled concerns, with economists openly discussing the prospect of recession.

The Reserve Bank (RBA) has said public trust is under strain after five years of strong inflation, which is not expected to return to a normal 2.5% until mid-2028.

With a long wait ahead, households are starting to ask how much worse it will get.

Cracks beneath the surface

When the RBA this month lifted its cash rate to its highest level since 2008, the governor, Michele Bullock, said she couldn’t yet see the economy “cracking” under the strain.

That week, household spending kept growing, with particular strength in electronic goods, and eating and drinking out, according to the Commonwealth Bank (CBA). The RBA expects the economy to grow by at least 1% next year, helped by steady spending.

But consumer confidence has slumped to levels typically seen during recessions, Westpac surveys show, meaning that how Australians feel does not seem to match the economy’s outward strength.

The national debt helpline’s coordinator, Vicki Staff, says the weakness has been felt beneath the surface this year. A record 190,000 people called the helpline in the year to August. The surge began as soon as the helpline reopened in January after the Christmas break, well before the Iran war began or interest rates began rising, Staff says.

“We knew something was up right from the beginning, and then we’ve just seen it deteriorate from there,” she says. “People are terrified of losing their homes, or their cars.”

Australians with no financial buffers left have told the helpline they are taking desperate measures to make their repayments: skipping medical appointments, leaving prescriptions unfilled, leaving the car in the driveway, cancelling their children’s out-of-school activities.

“They’re skipping meals,” Staff says. “People are having to rely on food banks a lot more because you can’t ask a supermarket for a hardship arrangement.”

People have not been counted in financial stress data because they are making desperate efforts to keep on top of repayments, Staff says.

This week, that began to change. CBA on Wednesday reported the share of its customers behind on their mortgage repayments had climbed to a 12-year high.

ANZ reported the share of customers 90 days behind on mortgage repayments hit a five-year high of 0.95%. Its chief executive, Nuno Matos, told parliament on Thursday the number of customers in hardship arrangements had risen 10% in the last six months.

“We should expect those [arrears] numbers to continue to deteriorate,” Matos said. “I don’t expect them to go to a historically bad place, but they will get worse before they get better.”

The founder of House You housing justice organisation, Chels Hood Withey, says people who work the hardest are doing it the toughest, while “rent is too damn high and mortgages are crushing families”.

Hood Withey urged the government to prioritise housing as a human right, including scaling up the public housing available for people who couldn’t afford private rentals.

“Millions of people would have a secure home, and when your home is secure, everything else gets easier: your health, your work, your ability to plan a life,” they said.

Stress and cuts

Financial stress is contributing to Australian society becoming more divided and pessimistic about the future, according to the Scanlon Foundation social cohesion report for 2026, a study now in its 20th year.

The survey of 10,000 adults found 40% of people were dissatisfied with their financial situation, and 30% went without meals, could not pay the rent or mortgage, could not heat or cool their home or could not pay for medicines or healthcare often or sometimes in the last 12 months.

The Scanlon Foundation chief executive officer, Anthea Hancocks, says financial stress is lowering people’s sense of belonging and trust in others.

Nevertheless, Hancocks stresses that people should remember there are “sources of optimism” to be found, even if things feel hard at the moment.

“We know Australians feel a greater sense of belonging in their local area and feel comfortable with the diversity in their local area,” she says. “Most of the strength of our social cohesion comes from what’s happening in our local areas.”

When confidence in the economy was last this bad in 2022, unemployment was still below 4%, another source of optimism. But a slowing economy has seen jobs growth stall and brought unemployment up to 4.7%. It’s expected to reach 5% – back to where it was before the Covid pandemic.

Australia has also seen a series of high-profile redundancy rounds, after the National Australia Bank in October announced it would cut 2,500 jobs and design platform Canva cut 1,200 jobs. The country’s biggest airline, Qantas, this week said it would scrap 850 Australian jobs.

And while falling house prices have so far helped affordability, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority on Thursday warned “substantial” job losses could snowball into a “more severe” financial shock.

The deputy chief economist at AMP, Diana Mousina, says unemployment will probably hit 5% by July, but is still historically low and conditions are better than they were in the 1990s.

Mousina says households have been worn down by four years of high inflation and are starting to blame the government and RBA for failing to fix it.

“[People] think, well, I can’t change interest rates,” she says. “I can’t change the fuel price, there’s so little that’s in my control. I’m at the whim of government or the central bank or politicians overseas determining my livelihood.”

But AMP expects Australia to avoid recession and mass job cuts, with most people only facing a longer gap to find new jobs and slower wage growth.

“There will be people that are going to lose work due to the slowdown in economic growth, but hopefully the economy is strong enough to absorb those people,” Mousina says. “We still have pockets of growth, but clearly our economy is slowing.”

australia.title: Pride and no prejudice: how Tough Guy Book Club taught 10,000 men to be unashamed of reading
australia.snippet: When founder Shay Leighton put fliers in tattoo parlours, barbers and boxing gyms in Australia, men quickly responded – then it went glob...
australia.content:
“When did we decide that men and reading and toughness all had to be separate things?” Shay Leighton asks over a pint of Melbourne Black in his local Brunswick pub. “I don’t know about you, but I didn’t get a vote.”

For 14 years, Leighton has run the Tough Guy Book Club, a not-for-profit charity dedicated to encouraging men to read – although he’s quick to stress that they do more than just that. “We’re not a reading club, we’re a talking club,” he says. “The three goals of book club are: read more, talk more, have more friends.”

Leighton was once a tough kid himself but in 2012 he found himself in need of purpose: “I’d made some pretty bad choices and I was really unhappy. My partner had just left, my business had closed down and I didn’t have any friends.” A book club was a way “to get me out of the house cause I had pretty much fucked my life up”.

At the start, the club was just Leighton and his mate Tom Scott. As they sat discussing their first book – Ernest Hemingway’s The Old Man and the Sea – in the beer garden of a Collingwood pub, they had an encounter that would change everything. A stranger, “a big guy, a neck-tat dude”, approached and asked if they were in a book club. When Leighton confirmed they were, certain that he was about to get punched in the head, the man immediately asked, “Can I join?”

“We just invited people who didn’t think they were invited,” Leighton says. “And we invited people in places where they didn’t usually get invited.”

When they put fliers up in tattoo parlours, men’s barbers and boxing gyms, the interest was immediate: Tough Guy Book Club now runs chapters in 10 countries and has 10,000 members worldwide. Individual chapters are organised and run locally, meeting at 7pm on the first Wednesday of every month.

As for the name, several variations were tried out but “every time I said Tough Guy Book Club and someone laughed, I got more and more determined to call it that”, Leighton says. “Because those two things, toughness and reading, for some reason they’ve become so separate that, when you push them together, people think you’re doing comedy.”

Incongruity is a powerful weapon and a great recruitment tool but it can also reinforce cultural stereotypes around literacy and masculinity, something Leighton is fighting to change. “I’m not what a reader looks like,” he says. “I’m not invited to the local literary festival.” The typical Tough Guy Book Club member “is not telling you he wants to read more; he’s not walking around bookstores”. The focus is determinedly analogue, too; the club is only held “in person, at the pub and in your neighbourhood. We don’t want to do meetings online.”

For former NRL player and BookTok sensation Luke Bateman, the online space was an essential conduit to the world of reading and a lifeline when he was at his lowest. After a well-publicised breakdown brought on by a gambling addiction, Bateman retreated to his family farm, where a single book-related post on TikTok – recorded from his tractor – went viral. He clocks that down to incongruity, too.

“It’s unexpected that someone who looks like me and has my background would be so in love with reading and want to promote it so passionately,” he says, over the phone from Brisbane. “I’ve read since I was a child; it’s a genuine and authentic part of me. Reading transports me to somewhere I can exist without fear of ridicule. I just get to experience a deep sense of joy.”

It wasn’t always the case, though. As soon as Bateman was catapulted into the world of professional rugby, he learned to repress his love of reading, and certainly would never let a teammate see him with a book. “I had a lot of shame around my reading. I never saw men read. Reading was a feminine thing. Young boys need to see men read, see their heroes and role models share a love of literature.”

The biggest barrier to men reading is other men. And it happens early. In his podcast In The Good Books, Bateman talks to children’s author Scott Stuart about a study on boys’ reading that illuminates something essential about boys and their relationship with books. When boys are asked to choose a book for themselves, “gender doesn’t enter the equation”, Stuart explains. It can be pink, it can be about fairies, boys don’t care. “But when they are asked to choose for other boys, suddenly all the female main characters disappear.”

While reading rates are declining among men and women in Australia – gen X men are the only demographic that reads statistically less than women of the same age – Bateman believes passionately that we can turn those numbers around if we start in the home.

“If you want your kids to be readers, you have to be a reader. We can’t be placing the responsibilities of failing literacy rates upon children. As adults, that’s our responsibility; we’re the ones failing them. We live in a world that corporations and capitalism have wanted to make very easy for us, frictionless. But reading requires friction, a little bit more effort.”

Bateman thinks books are essential “if we want our children to grow and prosper and evolve into fully integrated and capable, competent human beings”.

Leighton sees the transformational effects of reading in men firsthand. He runs a book club in a prison – they also started with The Old Man and the Sea – and he encourages them to join Tough Guy Book Club once they’re out.

“When you’ve done 15 years, the only other guys you know are guys who’ve done 15 years. I just wanted to give them another option. They can come hang out with us.”

When men read, the whole community benefits. Bateman believes that reading lets young men see “that there are further possibilities for them outside the narrative they’ve been given”. For Leighton, men must actively tear down their own assumptions about reading and masculinity – because no one else can do it for them.

“Men are our own jailers and our own police officers on this,” he says. “Somewhere along the way we decided and then we just enforced it ourselves. We’re the only people who can help us out of that.”

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

world.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
world.snippet: President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and...
world.content:
Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry.

An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

The health ministry gave the casualty toll, adding more than 70 of the injured were discharged after receiving treatment.

Train derailments and crashes are common in Egypt, where the railway system has a history of mismanagement and poor maintenance of equipment. In recent years the government has announced modernisation initiatives to improve its railways.

Ayman Gamal, a resident of Kafr Girza in al-Ayyat where the crash occurred, said people rushed to the scene, pulled out survivors and called ambulances.

Gamal said he saw about 80 of the injured being taken by ambulances to hospital. Some passengers were trapped inside one of the carriages of the stationary train and died, he said.

Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation.

Outside al-Wasta central hospital in Beni Suef province, where some of the injured were taken for treatment, survivors said passengers were in shock and struggling to breathe because of all the dust that was kicked up. Nearby villagers eventually got them out, they said.

Farha Gamal, a survivor who was inside the Fayyoum train, said she saw some of the passengers who appeared dead and others were struggling to find their way out of the car. “There were other cars that were completely mangled,” she said in an interview.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the crash site to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

Egypt’s deadliest train crash was in 2002 when more than 300 people were killed after a fire broke out on an overnight train journeying from Cairo to southern Egypt.

world.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
world.snippet: See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and...
world.content:
African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.

See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

world.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
world.snippet: Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families The l...
world.content:
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting
